extracted.intended_audience: patent agents, patent attorneys, trademark attorneys, and other practitioners who practice before the USPTO (OED audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, definitions, investigatory procedures, and ethical standards governing practice before the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO), as administered by the Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED). Intended to guide practitioner conduct, supervisory obligations, privilege issues, and discipline process outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary jurisdiction (37 C.F.R. § 11.19(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifies who is subject to OED disciplinary jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes all practitioners engaged in practice before the Office; administratively suspended; registered to practice before the Office in patent cases; inactivated; authorized under § 11.6(d) to take testimony; or transferred to disability inactive status, reprimanded, suspended, or excluded from practice by a duly constituted authority (including USPTO Director). Practitioners who resigned remain subject for conduct prior to resignation and for any practice after resignation. Non-registered persons who provide or offer to provide legal services before the Office are also subject to disciplinary authority (37 C.F.R. § 11.19(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Practitioner' (37 C.F.R. § 11.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Who counts as a 'practitioner' for OED rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes: (1) attorneys or agents registered to practice before the Office in patent matters; (2) individuals authorized under 5 U.S.C. 500(b) or § 11.14(a)-(c) to practice in trademark or non-patent matters; (3) individuals authorized to practice before the Office in a patent case or under § 11.9(a) or (b); and (4) individuals authorized under § 11.16(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice before the Office — general (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: What 'practice before the Office' encompasses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encompasses law-related services connected with presentations to the Office relating to clients' rights, privileges, duties, or responsibilities under laws/regulations administered by the Office for patents, trademarks, enrollment, or discipline. Examples: preparing documents in contemplation of filing, corresponding/communicating with the Office, representing a client in documents/interviews/hearings/meetings, advising clients on matters pending or contemplated to be presented before the Office. Practitioners may employ non-practitioner assistants under their supervision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice before the Office — patent matters (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific patent-related activities that constitute practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes: preparing and prosecuting patent applications; consulting/advising clients in contemplation of filing patent applications or other documents with the Office; drafting specifications or claims; drafting amendments or replies that may require written argument to establish patentability; drafting replies to Office communications regarding patent applications; drafting communications for public use, interference, reexamination, petitions, appeals to or proceedings before the PTAB, or other proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice before the Office — trademark matters (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)(2) & § 11.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific trademark/non-patent activities that constitute practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes: consulting/advising clients in contemplation of filing trademark applications or other documents with the Office; preparing and prosecuting trademark registration applications; preparing amendments that may require written argument to establish registrability; conducting opposition, cancellation, concurrent use proceedings, or appeals to the TTAB. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.14 for who may practice in trademark and other non-patent matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grievance definition and OED investigation process (37 C.F.R. § 11.1, § 11.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: How disciplinary investigations begin and who may be asked to provide information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'grievance' is a written submission to the OED Director presenting possible grounds for discipline of a specified practitioner (37 C.F.R. § 11.1). In investigating a grievance, the OED Director may request information and evidence from the grievant, the practitioner, and any person reasonably expected to provide information needed for the investigation (37 C.F.R. § 11.22(f)(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible investigation outcomes and referral to Committee on Discipline (37 C.F.R. § 11.22(h), § 11.32, § 11.34(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: What the OED Director may do at conclusion of an investigation and timing limits for complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upon conclusion the Director may: close the investigation without action; issue a warning; institute formal charges (with Committee on Discipline approval); or enter into a settlement agreement and submit to the USPTO Director for approval (37 C.F.R. § 11.22(h)). If grounds exist, matters may be referred to the Committee on Discipline for probable cause determination (37 C.F.R. § 11.32). Timing: complaints must be filed within one year after the date the OED Director receives a grievance; no complaint may be filed more than 10 years after the misconduct date (37 C.F.R. § 11.34(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal discipline and interim suspension (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.24, 11.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discipline based on actions in other jurisdictions and interim suspension criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reciprocal discipline may be based on discipline by a state or federal program/agency and is often handled on documentary record only (37 C.F.R. § 11.24). Interim suspension may be imposed based on conviction of a serious crime, with referral to a hearing officer for determination of final disciplinary action (37 C.F.R. § 11.25).

rubrics_metrics.name: OED Diversion Pilot Program eligibility criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for diverting practitioners to a treatment/assistance program instead of formal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria include: willingness and ability to participate; no public discipline by USPTO or another jurisdiction in the past three years; and the misconduct must not involve misappropriation of funds or dishonesty/fraud/deceit/misrepresentation; must not result or be likely to result in substantial prejudice to a client/other person; must not constitute a 'serious crime'; and must not be part of a pattern of similar misconduct or same nature as misconduct for which practitioner was disciplined within past five years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed annual active practitioner fee and CLE proposal (NPRM 84 Fed. Reg. 37398)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals concerning fees and continuing legal education for patent practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (July 31, 2019) proposed no paper filing option and a voluntary CLE: six hours of CLE every 24 months — five hours patent law and practice and one hour ethics. (This slide reports the NPRM; check final rules for adoption and effective dates.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of U.S. attorney for foreign-domiciled trademark applicants (Final rule 84 Fed. Reg. 31498)
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign-domiciled parties' representation requirements in trademark matters before the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective Aug. 3, 2019, foreign-domiciled trademark applicants, registrants, and parties to TTAB proceedings must be represented at the USPTO by an attorney licensed to practice law in the United States. Consequences: Canadian patent agents may no longer represent Canadian parties in U.S. trademark matters (they may serve only as additionally-appointed practitioners); clients must appoint U.S.-licensed attorney for formal responses; USPTO will correspond only with U.S.-licensed attorneys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Pro Bono Program purpose and coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Program goals and coverage for assisting under-resourced inventors and small businesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assists financially under-resourced independent inventors and small businesses per AIA § 32; promotes small business growth; helps ensure deserving inventions are not without patent protection due to lack of funds for counsel. 50-state coverage achieved and maintained since Aug. 2015; practitioners and inventors can find regional programs on USPTO website.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of patent-agent privilege (case law guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: When communications with patent agents are protected by privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit (In re Queen's Univ.) recognized privilege only for activities patent agents are authorized to perform (see 37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)(1)). Privilege is narrower than attorney-client privilege and applies where communications are reasonably necessary and incident to prosecution. Documents not 'reasonably necessary and incident to' prosecution (e.g., communications performed as part of product development or to develop new formulations rather than to seek patent protection) may not be protected (Onyx Therapeutics). State law may vary (In re Silver/Texas example). Also note specific rulemaking re: attorney-client privilege for PTAB trials (82 Fed. Reg. 51570).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized Practice of Law (UPL) — examples and rule highlights
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of conduct constituting UPL and related disciplinary rule citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples (e.g., In re Campbell) indicate UPL occurs where patent agents hold themselves out as attorneys, practice outside authorized scope, or represent clients in non-USPTO matters without authority. Rule highlights cited: dishonesty/fraud/deceit/misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4)); conduct prejudicial to administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5)); holding oneself out to be an attorney or lawyer (37 C.F.R. § 10.31(d)(1)); intentional/habitual violation of disciplinary rules (37 C.F.R. § 10.89(c)(6)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to supervise / aiding unauthorized practice (rule set)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner responsibilities relating to supervision of non-practitioner assistants and prohibition on aiding UPL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples (In re Swyers, In re Crabtree, In re Chow) show discipline where practitioners permitted non-attorneys to perform substantive work with little/no supervision, failed to maintain escrow/trust accounts, or failed to disclose referral/payment arrangements. Relevant rules: competence (37 C.F.R. § 11.101); safekeeping property (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.115(a) & (c)); candor toward tribunal (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1)); responsibilities regarding non-practitioner assistance (37 C.F.R. § 11.503); aiding UPL (37 C.F.R. § 11.505).

rubrics_metrics.name: Misrepresentation, filing fraudulent specimens, and cooperating with OED investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct that triggers discipline for misrepresentations and failures to cooperate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include filing fraudulent/manipulated trademark specimens, permitting non-attorneys to sign applications, failing to deposit client funds in trust accounts, and failing to cooperate with OED investigations (In re Swyers). Rule highlights: conduct prejudicial to administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5)); giving false or misleading information to the Office (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(2)(ii)). Outcomes can include exclusion on consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification requirements for papers presented to the Office (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: What a party certifies when presenting papers to the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By presenting any paper, the submitting party certifies statements of their own knowledge are true; that to the best of their knowledge, information, and belief formed after reasonable inquiry, allegations and factual contentions have evidentiary support or are likely to after reasonable opportunity for investigation/discovery; and denials of factual contentions are warranted on the evidence or reasonably based on lack of information or belief (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark Post-Registration Proof of Use Audit Program criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: When a trademark registration may be selected for a post-registration audit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permanent audit program (launched Nov. 1, 2017). A registration may be audited if: (1) a Section 8 or 71 declaration of use is filed; and (2) the registration includes at least one class with four or more goods/services, or at least two classes with two or more goods/services. If audited, proof of use for additional goods/services in the registration will be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect, candor, and disreputable/gross misconduct (case guidance and rule citations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples and rules related to neglecting client matters and lack of candor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: In re Kroll — failed to file client's application, poor docketing, posted invention for sale, filed late (20 months after posting). Aggravating factors include prior discipline; penalties included suspension/exclusion. Rule highlights: disreputable or gross misconduct (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a)); certification upon submitting papers (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)); neglect (37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deceit and conduct prejudicial to administration of justice (case guidance and rule citations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of deceitful conduct and relevant disciplinary rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: In re Kroll (separate proceeding) — offered money-back guarantees, amended claims/specification without client authorization, paid clients not to file ethics grievances, and other deceitful conduct leading to exclusion. Rule highlights: giving false or misleading information to a client in connection with USPTO business (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(2)(i)); conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5) & 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d)). Aggravating factors (e.g., prior history) increase severity of discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to and publication of disciplinary decisions and notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Where to find decisions imposing public discipline and Official Gazette notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions imposing public discipline are available in the FOIA Reading Room (https://foiadocuments.uspto.gov/oed/) and in the Official Gazette for Patents (www.uspto.gov/news/og/patent_og/index.jsp). The Official Gazette includes published formal matters and notices; use links to 'Notices' in each issue.
